promptText: Why does `assertEquals("BILLING", triageService.classify(ticket))` become a brittle test once an LLM is involved?
options: Because JUnit cannot compare String values reliably

Because the model call is non-deterministic and can shift with provider-side updates or prompt tweaks, so an exact-match assertion built against an inherently non-deterministic collaborator breaks intermittently even when the code is correct
Because classify() always returns a numeric confidence score, never a string
Because Spring AI does not support returning String values from a ChatClient call
explanation: Exact-match assertions against live model output are the single most common testing mistake described in the chapter — they fail intermittently for reasons unrelated to your own code being wrong.

promptText: What is a 'golden dataset' (eval set) in the context of AI testing?
options: A dataset used exclusively to fine-tune the production model
A curated, version-controlled collection of representative inputs, each paired with a reference answer, rubric, or acceptance criteria, used for statistical regression testing
A snapshot of the vector database taken once per release
The set of prompts that received the highest user satisfaction ratings
explanation: The golden dataset is the AI-era equivalent of a regression test suite, graded statistically rather than compared with equals(), and it grows as production reveals new failure modes.

promptText: Which layer of the AI testing pyramid should structural validity of a model's JSON output ('does it parse against the schema at all') be tested at?
options: LLM-as-judge evaluation, since parsing quality is subjective
Human review, since only a person can confirm valid JSON
A deterministic assertion — the chapter states this should almost always be a hard deterministic check, not a statistical one
It cannot be tested automatically at any layer
explanation: Structural validity (JSON parses against the target schema) is one of the cheapest, most deterministic properties to check and should be a hard pass/fail assertion, not folded into a statistical or judge-based layer.

promptText: According to the chapter's historical background, what was the well-documented weakness of BLEU and ROUGE as evaluation metrics?
options: They required a live internet connection to compute
They measured surface-level lexical (n-gram) overlap with reference text, not semantic correctness or factual accuracy
They could only be applied to code generation tasks, never natural language
They were replaced entirely by precision and recall before LLMs existed
explanation: BLEU/ROUGE score n-gram overlap; a summary can score well while subtly misrepresenting the source, and a valid alternative phrasing can score poorly — the direct motivation for semantic similarity and LLM-as-judge approaches.

promptText: In Spring AI, how can you unit test a service that depends on a ChatClient without making a real network call?
options: It is not possible; every ChatClient-dependent test requires a live provider call
Mock the underlying ChatModel with Mockito to return a fixed ChatResponse, then build a ChatClient from that mock and inject it into the service under test
Set spring.ai.test-mode=true in application.yml to auto-stub all model calls
Use @SpringBootTest exclusively, since ChatModel cannot be mocked with plain Mockito
explanation: Because ChatModel is an interface, it mocks like any other Spring dependency — no special AI-testing library is required for fully deterministic unit tests of business logic around the model call.

promptText: What does the chapter identify as the correct way to grow a golden dataset over the life of a system?
options: Regenerate it from scratch every quarter using only synthetic examples
Append every real production failure surfaced by observability or user reports as a new permanent regression example, exactly like a production bug becoming a regression test
Keep it frozen at whatever the team thought to test on day one, to preserve baseline comparability
Only add examples that score perfectly on the current model, to keep the baseline high
explanation: The chapter draws a direct parallel to traditional regression testing: every real user-reported or observability-surfaced failure should become a permanent golden dataset entry, compounding the suite's value over time.

promptText: A golden-dataset regression run shows the new prompt's faithfulness score dropped from 0.87 to 0.86. According to the chapter's statistical guidance, what should you do before concluding this is a real regression?
options: Immediately block the PR, since any decrease indicates a regression
Ignore the score entirely, since golden-dataset metrics are inherently untrustworthy
Check the natural run-to-run spread (e.g., by running multiple trials) to see whether the observed change is within the noise floor before treating it as a real signal
Switch immediately to a different judge model, since the current one must be miscalibrated
explanation: Aggregate metrics are sample statistics carrying sampling uncertainty; a small drop within the observed natural spread across repeated runs is not distinguishable from noise, whereas a drop with non-overlapping ranges is a real signal.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that testing RAG generation with a hand-picked 'good' context gives false confidence?
options: Because hand-picked contexts always exceed the model's context window limit
Because it tests a scenario that cannot occur in production, where retrieval is imperfect — faithfulness under real, imperfect retrieval is what actually needs validating
Because hand-picked contexts cannot be serialized into a golden dataset file format
Because LLM-as-judge scoring requires randomly generated context, not curated context
explanation: The chapter explicitly separates retrieval testing from generation testing; testing generation against artificially perfect context that retrieval would never actually produce hides real faithfulness regressions under realistic, imperfect retrieval.

promptText: In the layered CI architecture (Section 8), which tests should run on every single commit, and which should be gated behind prompt/model-affecting changes or a schedule?
options: LLM-as-judge evaluation on every commit; deterministic unit tests only on a nightly schedule
Deterministic unit and contract/schema tests on every commit; golden-dataset regression and judge-model evaluation gated to PRs touching prompts/models or run on a schedule/pre-release
All tests, including full production-model golden-dataset runs, should run identically on every commit for maximum safety
Human review should run automatically on every commit via a bot
explanation: Deterministic, free, instant tests belong at the per-commit gate; real-model golden-dataset and judge-model runs cost real money and time, so they're reserved for prompt/model-affecting PRs or scheduled/pre-release runs.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend periodically recalibrating an LLM-as-judge against human-labeled samples?
options: Because judge models are legally required to be re-certified every quarter

Because the judge model is itself an unverified dependency subject to provider-side updates and its own non-determinism — exactly analogous to periodically auditing a spam filter's precision against manually reviewed emails
Because human review is strictly more accurate than any automated method and should replace LLM-as-judge entirely
Because recalibration is only needed once, at initial deployment, never again afterward
explanation: A judge model can drift the same way any model can; spot-checking its scores against human judgment on a regular cadence, especially after judge-model version changes, keeps its grading trustworthy.

promptText: A contract test feeds a `BeanOutputConverter` several realistic response variants: raw JSON, markdown-fenced JSON, and JSON preceded by conversational prose ('Sure! Here is...'). What is this test actually verifying?
options: That the model always produces perfectly formatted JSON with no variation
That the output converter can extract and parse the target type correctly across a range of realistic (including slightly messy) model response shapes, rather than only the ideal case
That the ChatModel mock correctly simulates network latency
That the golden dataset contains at least three examples per category
explanation: Contract tests verify that a range of plausible real-world response shapes either parse correctly or fail in a handled way, since models don't always emit perfectly clean structured output on the first try.

promptText: Why does the chapter warn against using only LLM-as-judge and skipping cheaper deterministic checks?
options: Because LLM-as-judge is factually incapable of detecting any quality issues

Because judge-model calls are slow and cost real money per run; a structural JSON-schema failure should be caught by a free, instant deterministic assertion rather than discovered later by an expensive judge call that never gets to evaluate content quality
Because Spring AI's Evaluator interface does not support being called more than once per test
Because deterministic checks always produce more accurate quality scores than any judge model
explanation: The layered pyramid principle is to move down to the cheapest reliable layer for each property; skipping deterministic schema checks wastes an expensive judge call on inputs that were already structurally broken.

promptText: The chapter presents two sets of 5 trial runs: baseline spread 0.85–0.89, new prompt spread 0.82–0.85. What conclusion does it draw, and what is the underlying statistical reasoning?
options: No conclusion can be drawn because 5 trials is never a large enough sample for any inference

This is very likely a real regression, because the two ranges barely overlap — if the new spread had instead fully overlapped the baseline's noise floor, no difference could be concluded from that sample size alone
The new prompt is an improvement because a lower score with tighter variance is always preferable
The two spreads are considered statistically identical because they differ by less than 0.05
explanation: The chapter's example treats each aggregate score as a sample statistic carrying uncertainty; near-non-overlapping spreads across repeated trials indicate a real effect, whereas overlapping spreads would mean the difference is within noise.

promptText: For a content-moderation classifier, the chapter argues that a single blanket accuracy number can be dangerously misleading. Why, and what should pass/fail thresholds be based on instead?
options: Because accuracy cannot be computed for classification tasks at all, only for generation tasks

Because a system can have 95% overall accuracy while still failing unacceptably on the small fraction of cases that matter most (e.g., false negatives on genuinely harmful content); thresholds should be set per-class based on the cost asymmetry between false positives and false negatives
Because accuracy is only meaningful when computed on the full production traffic, never on a golden dataset
Because moderation classifiers should never be evaluated with automated metrics, only human review
explanation: The chapter explicitly revives the classical ML lesson that false negatives and false positives often carry very different costs (e.g., missing harmful content vs. flagging benign content), so per-class, cost-weighted thresholds (like F1) are needed instead of a single blanket accuracy figure.

promptText: A team ships a prompt rewrite that improves the golden-dataset faithfulness score by 2% but doubles token usage and P95 latency. According to the chapter, why is a quality-only evaluation gate insufficient to catch this as a regression, and what should the harness track instead?
options: It's not actually a problem, since any faithfulness improvement should be shipped regardless of cost or latency impact

A quality-only gate only measures one dimension; latency and cost must be tracked as first-class regression metrics stored alongside quality scores in the same baseline file, so a quality-for-cost trade-off is visible in the same review rather than discovered later
The chapter recommends this trade-off is always acceptable as long as the model version is pinned
This scenario cannot occur because token usage and faithfulness scores are mathematically linked
explanation: Ignoring cost and latency until after a prompt change ships is listed as a common mistake; the chapter recommends tracking P50/P95 latency and token cost alongside quality scores in the same baseline so a quality-for-cost trade is visible in the same review as the quality delta.
